title: What the Specification Did Not Say: Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language

Title:What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Coding-agent benchmarks often describe a task in natural language but grade it with tests taken from the upstream project. Passing those tests can require information the description never states: a constant's name, a module path, an exact message. We call this a specification-oracle gap: where it exists, a benchmark also measures whether an agent reproduces upstream implementation details. We formalise the gap, including the inconsistencies that chains of dependent tasks add, and build a static audit for five languages that classifies every name-, path- and literal-level dependency of every scored test (held-out precision 89.2%, recall 92.9%). On SWE-Milestone (98 graded milestones, 35 published runs), 25 milestones contain a test that depends on an unstated, non-inferable name or path. Build units with such a dependency fail in 80.6% of runs, against 48.4% for comparable units without one, and withholding a single hidden name from the reference stops its unit's tests from compiling in 126 of 128 cases. The leaderboard's ranking is robust to removing the affected tests, but they shift scores within repositories and favour agents that reproduce upstream names. Across four further benchmarks, prevalence appears to follow construction: a third or more of the tasks are affected where specifications are release notes or LLM summaries, almost none where tasks are screened or written for their tests; how much a gap costs depends on how the harness grades. We release the audit, corrected filter lists and specification addenda.

report.summary: A new audit finds coding-agent benchmarks often require unstated upstream names or paths, inflating failures and favoring agents that reproduce implementation details.
report.background: Coding-agent benchmarks typically pair a natural-language task description with tests borrowed from the real upstream project. That setup is convenient and realistic, but the tests can encode details the description never supplies: exact constants, module paths, error messages, or file names. When passing requires guessing those upstream choices, the benchmark measures implementation recall as well as coding ability. The problem grows as benchmarks are built quickly from release notes, issue threads, or LLM-generated summaries, and as agents are ranked on pass rates. The paper formalises this specification-oracle gap and audits how often scored tests depend on information absent from the task specification.
key_points: The authors define the specification-oracle gap and build a static audit for five languages that classifies every name-, path- and literal-level dependency in scored tests. On held-out data it reaches 89.2% precision and 92.9% recall, making the gap measurable rather than anecdotal.

On SWE-Milestone, 25 of 98 graded milestones contain a test that depends on an unstated, non-inferable name or path. Build units with such a dependency fail in 80.6% of runs, versus 48.4% for comparable units without one; withholding a single hidden name blocks compilation in 126 of 128 cases.

Removing affected tests leaves the overall leaderboard ranking robust, but scores shift within repositories and favour agents that reproduce upstream names. The gap therefore distorts comparisons between agents and can reward memorisation of implementation details over genuine problem-solving.

Across four further benchmarks, prevalence tracks how tasks were built: a third or more are affected when specifications are release notes or LLM summaries, and almost none where tasks are screened or written alongside their tests. How much a gap costs also depends on the grading harness.
report.impact: The findings challenge the validity of test-graded coding-agent leaderboards. For the AI industry, they show that benchmark scores can conflate specification-following with upstream recall, so claims about agent capability need audits and clearer task specifications. For developers building or using benchmarks, the practical step is to check whether scored tests require unstated constants, paths, or messages, and to separate those dependencies from intended task requirements. For regular users, the takeaway is that a coding agent's high pass rate may not translate into robust performance on underspecified real-world tasks; benchmark design, not just model quality, shapes the trust users place in these tools.
report.tools: Follow the paper's released static audit, corrected filter lists, and specification addenda, and apply them to SWE-Milestone-style harnesses. For follow-up work, combine tree-sitter or Semgrep with test-file analysis to flag hidden names, paths, and literals; run agents in spec-only versus test-graded modes; and compare results on SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Watch projects that publish task specifications alongside tests rather than reusing upstream tests without screening.
